name: Graphs and Union-Find Interview Prep
description: 20 advanced questions on graph traversal, shortest paths, topological ordering, connectivity, and union-find optimization.

cards.front: 1. What makes a problem a graph problem?
cards.back: If the entities have relationships, paths, or reachability that matter to the answer, it is probably a graph problem. Cycles and multiple valid traversal paths are the telltale signs.

cards.front: 2. When should you use BFS instead of DFS?
cards.back: Use BFS when you need shortest paths in an unweighted graph or level-by-level exploration. DFS is better when you need deep exploration, cycle detection, or exhaustive search.

cards.front: 3. Why does graph traversal usually need a visited set?
cards.back: Because graphs can contain cycles and repeated paths, which would otherwise cause infinite loops or repeated work. The visited set is what keeps traversal finite and efficient.

cards.front: 4. What is topological sorting used for?
cards.back: It gives a valid order of processing for a directed acyclic graph where dependencies must come first. It is commonly used for task scheduling, build systems, and dependency resolution.

cards.front: 5. How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
cards.back: You can use DFS with a recursion stack or a topological-sort-based approach. The key is to distinguish nodes that are fully processed from nodes currently being explored.

cards.front: 6. What is the difference between directed and undirected graph traversal?
cards.back: Directed graphs only allow movement along edge direction, while undirected graphs allow traversal both ways. That changes connectivity, cycle detection, and sometimes the storage representation.

cards.front: 7. Why are shortest-path problems not all the same?
cards.back: Different edge weights require different algorithms and assumptions. Unweighted shortest path is a BFS problem, while weighted graphs may require Dijkstra or a different approach altogether.

cards.front: 8. When is Dijkstra appropriate?
cards.back: Use it when all edge weights are non-negative and you need single-source shortest paths. Negative weights break its assumptions.

cards.front: 9. What problem does union-find solve?
cards.back: It tracks dynamic connectivity: whether elements belong to the same connected component. That makes it useful for component counting, cycle detection, and Kruskal-style minimum spanning tree construction.

cards.front: 10. Why is path compression important in union-find?
cards.back: It shortens the tree structure after finds, so future operations are much faster. Combined with union by rank or size, it keeps the amortized cost near constant.

cards.front: 11. What is the difference between connected components and strongly connected components?
cards.back: Connected components are used in undirected graphs and care about reachability ignoring direction, while strongly connected components require mutual reachability in directed graphs. The notion of connectivity changes with edge direction.

cards.front: 12. Why can graph problems become expensive quickly?
cards.back: Because the number of nodes and edges can create large state spaces, especially when traversal branches widely or repeatedly revisits states. Without pruning or memoization, performance can degrade fast.

cards.front: 13. What is the key difference between adjacency lists and adjacency matrices?
cards.back: Adjacency lists are space-efficient for sparse graphs, while adjacency matrices provide constant-time edge checks but use much more memory. The right choice depends on density and query pattern.

cards.front: 14. How do you think about multi-source BFS?
cards.back: It starts traversal from several origins at once, which is useful for nearest-source or distance-to-any-source problems. It is still BFS, but seeded differently.

cards.front: 15. What is the danger of forgetting to mark visited at the right time?
cards.back: Marking too late can enqueue or recurse into the same node many times, which wastes work or even creates loops. In graph code, timing of the visited mark is often as important as the traversal order.

cards.front: 16. Why are topological order and cycle detection closely related?
cards.back: A directed graph has a topological order only if it is acyclic. If you cannot produce such an order, a cycle is present.

cards.front: 17. How do you model graph state in code safely?
cards.back: Keep the node identity, adjacency, and visitation state explicit so traversal logic is easy to reason about. Hidden state is where many graph bugs come from.

cards.front: 18. What is a common use case for union-find in real interviews?
cards.back: Detecting cycles or grouping connected items in a stream of edges is a common use. It is especially useful when the graph changes incrementally.

cards.front: 19. What are the most common graph implementation mistakes?
cards.back: Mixing up directed and undirected edges, forgetting visited tracking, using the wrong traversal for weighted paths, and mishandling disconnected components. Most bugs are representation bugs, not graph theory bugs.

cards.front: 20. When is a graph solution overkill?
cards.back: If the relationships are simple enough to flatten into a map or a few lookups, the graph machinery may be unnecessary. Choose the simplest model that captures the real dependency structure.

author: Gemini
